newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sasol sees more technology deals on way.
newsitem.headline: Sasol sees more technology deals on way.

text.p: South African fuel and chemicals firm Sasol Ltd said on Monday a recent burst of deals for its cutting edge conversion technology would be followed by The firm sealed agreement on Monday with Norway's Statoil on a technological alliance to convert natural gas into synthetic fuel using the firm's Fischer-Tropsch technique.
The move follows hot on the heels of an announcement in March that Sasol was in talks with Qatar Petroleum Corp on a similar joint venture to tap that country's abundant natural gas reserves.
"Those are not the only deals. We are talking to others and other projects are being considered," Sasol business development manager Cavan Hill told Reuters.
However, he said other deals in the pipeline were still at an early stage and declined to give a timescale for more announcements.
Sasol developed its expertise in the economic isolation of the apartheid era and became the white-run state's most effective sanctions buster by providing a way to make synthetic fuel from coal.
Sasol plants were a favoured target of African National Congress (ANC) fighters seeking to overthrow the racist state.
But now, as the democratic ANC-led South Africa has re-entered the world market, Sasol has found countries that once shunned it are knocking on the door seeking access to its technology.
"It is gratifying to see that international firms like Statoil are taking such interest," Hill said.

The two deals so far have given the firm access to the huge oil and gas fields of Northern Europe and the Mideast Gulf. Hill said the firm was looking to expand into areas such as Southeast Asia, West Africa and Latin America.
But he did not rule out further deals in Europe or the Gulf.
"There might be more in the Middle East or other parts of the world...you have to look for areas where there is low cost natural gas. It doesn't happen everywhere," he said.
Sasol's aim is to become a global player in the fuels industry and has rejected the idea of licensing out its technology, opting instead for partnerships with an equity element.
The Statoil deal will centre on developing floating Fischer-Tropsch conversion plants which could be placed on a ship or oil rig, converting the natural gas to synthetic crude.
These plants will be the first of their kind and, if the venture is successful, will be sold to other energy firms by a joint venture grouping in which Statoil and Sasol will take equity.
Hill said the market for the technology was already there, but development of the plants to the point of being put on sale could take several years.

Such facilities will allow the natural gas to be utilised at the point of production, rather than being piped ashore or back into the oil reservoir. This eliminates the flaring of natural gas and its associated environmental damage.
Sasol shares ended Monday up 25 cents to 52.00 rand.
